youtube.title: How Do You Know a Spider Is Asleep? | Toxic Tales
youtube.description:
How do you know a jumping spider is asleep, rather than just still?

In laboratory Portia fimbriata, researchers combined resting posture, twitching and retinal-tube movements with sound-response tests and a disrupted night. Thirty adults were tested in separate groups of ten per state. Four of ten in REM-like bouts did not react within ten seconds; all four later responded awake. Among responding spiders, estimated latencies were 4.27 seconds in REM-like bouts versus 1.69 seconds awake. Thirteen usable paired recordings showed mean total REM-like duration increasing from 9.4 to 16.9 minutes after fly disturbance. The disruption was not demonstrated complete deprivation; the results are group summaries, not individual trajectories. This is behavioral evidence, not proof of dreaming or neural equivalence to vertebrate REM sleep.

Geiger et al. (2026), PNAS 123(45):e2618030123. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2618030123
Open full text: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13752372/
Research evidence, limitations and credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-011.html
